title: The kidney stone
hook: in constant pain from stones, he writes about bearing illness (Essays 2.37)

segments.voice: Yesterday, of presumption: Montaigne listing his own faults, plainly and with a grin. Your line was my faults, plainly. Did you name one fault without beating yourself up over it? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-two.

What do you do with a pain that keeps coming back? Not one bad afternoon. A pain that arrives without warning, leaves, and returns when it pleases. Montaigne lived with one. He called it the stone: kidney stones, an illness he says he had dreaded long before it found him. In the essay on how children resemble their fathers, book two, chapter thirty-seven, he writes about living with it. He doesn't write as a saint, and he doesn't write as a doctor. He writes as a patient who is a little annoyed, a little curious, and still at his desk.
screen: `A PAIN THAT KEEPS COMING BACK.` → `HE CALLED IT THE STONE.` → `STILL AT HIS DESK.`

segments.voice: First, where it came from. Montaigne says his father had the stone too, and he can't get over it. How, he asks, could a tiny drop of seed carry the print of his father's illness, long before it ever showed? He doesn't pretend to know. It's the same shrug as what do I know, turned on his own body. Second, groan if you have to. He doesn't demand a brave face from himself. He writes, more or less, that if the body finds some relief in complaining, let it complain. What he guards is something else: that the pain not take over his judgment, that between the attacks he still thinks his own thoughts. The face can wince. The mind stays his. Third, the doctors. A large part of the essay pokes fun at the medicine of his own day: remedies that contradict each other, confident cures that don't cure. Hear that as a man of his time talking about the medicine of his time, not as advice about yours. His point is about being too sure, not about refusing help. Fourth, patience. Montaigne treats the stone almost like a stubborn houseguest. It comes, it goes, and he learns its habits. He even says the illness has been getting him used to the thought of dying, a little at a time. That isn't cheerful. But it's honest, and there's a steadiness in it. Patience with pain doesn't mean liking the pain. It means not adding a second fight, the fight against the fact that it's there, on top of the first. Closer to home, the pain might be a back, a headache, or a grief that flares on certain days. The stone's lesson is the same: let the body say ouch, and keep the mind your own.
screen: `FROM HIS FATHER, SOMEHOW.` · `GROAN IF YOU HAVE TO.` · `DOUBTING THE DOCTORS OF HIS DAY.` · `NO SECOND FIGHT.` · then, large: `PATIENT WITH PAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with one pain. Sit, and let the breath settle on its own. Find one place that aches, or one worry that hurts like an ache. Don't push it away, and don't make it bigger. Let it be exactly the size it is. If you want to sigh, sigh. Then notice what is still yours around it: the breath, the room, the next quiet thought. Two minutes of letting the pain be there without starting a second fight. The bell holds the time.
The kidney stone. Montaigne's unwelcome companion: let the body groan, and keep the mind your own. Today's word.

Your line: patient with pain. Today, when something hurts, say ouch if it helps, then ask what is still yours. That closes a week that ran from a fall off a horse, through books, cruelty, what do I know and the cat, to his faults and now the stone. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often turn to his pages on the stone as a picture of living with chronic pain: letting the body complain while keeping one's judgment steady.
